toc.title: When it's already been stirred up
Look at the flavor of the thought
Link it down to the body

blocks.p: What's the emotion, and what's the state, that is driving your thoughts? In my opinion, that is more significant than the thoughts themselves.

This came out of a question from one of my members. As she was moving into more safety, grief was coming up as she realized how familiar unsafety felt to her. Anger was coming up too. Part of what she was carrying came from an earlier experience that wasn't trauma informed at all: a one-day retreat where they went back through every stage of her development, dug out the emotions, and tried to clear them, one after another. She didn't have the safety to feel all of that. It was just too much. So her question was: what do you do with the grief and the emotions that come up, and how do you work with being re-traumatized by trauma work itself?

Here's an image that came up for me. As we anchor in safety and begin to look at the stuck defensive state, we don't want to push too far. So picture an army marching forward, little by little. Instead of rushing into battle and diving into trauma memories and parent stuff and whatever else, we just inch forward, slowly but surely. And every step of the way, we're anchoring in safety. Yes, go forward. Yes, go forward.
Every step you go forward, stuff is going to come up. Defensive stuff. Maybe it's grief or anger or loss, anxiety, flashbacks. It could be all kinds of things.

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.

blocks.h: When it's already been stirred up

blocks.p: But what if the army has already marched in? What if everything has already come up, and you can't un-know what was stirred up? We can't un-remember it. We can't exactly move backwards.

So we return to grounding and safety. That is the priority in everything I teach. As stuff comes up, memories or narratives or feelings, whatever it is: fine, okay, here it is. I see you. Let me stick you in my pocket. I'm going to ground in safety while you exist here. We can't ignore it. It is what it is. But we ground in safety until we get to a point where we can say, "Okay, now I'm ready to feel this a bit more."

And yes, you ground in safety before you do any work with your stuck defensive state, every time. In order to go into that work, you have to be able to sit with your feelings, which means you have to stay anchored in your safety state. That vagal brake has to be on. The safety work flows directly into the defense work. It's never really done, either. You keep practicing it and keep building the strength of your vagal brake.

I don't do parts work. I'm also an atheist. I'm super materialistic, extremely concrete: I exist right here, right now, my biology, my atoms, and that's about it. So when I hear spirituality and parts work and whatever else, in my mind I'm going, "Hold on. Bring it back to right here, right now, in the moment, in your body." If you want to add on the other stuff, fine. Run with it. I just can't do that for you. But can we share a language of what's happening right here, right now? That's what my work is: very concrete, what's really happening right here, right now.

The other thing that comes to mind is that dysregulation is dysregulation. We attribute it to a source: that practice I went to, that therapist who re-traumatized me, that one-day retreat. And yes, that sounds awful. We can validate that and agree.

But the dysregulation is the dysregulation. Rather than asking, "How do I re-regulate after being re-traumatized?", you're adding a layer onto it. Let's just bring it back to: you're dysregulated. Okay. Got it. The why of it adds a layer that I don't think is necessary when it really comes down to feeling what you're feeling.

Your body doesn't know why you're dysregulated. All it's doing is reacting. Your brain has a concept of why. It can attribute a story to it, and that story is valid. I'm not trying to invalidate it or minimize it. But when you look inward, your body is dysregulated. It's not attributing meaning to it.
As my member put it when this landed for her: removing the story takes away one more way to go into your head and stay out of your body. None of that really matters. Where am I right now?

blocks.h: Look at the flavor of the thought

blocks.p: When you start to look inward at your sensations, state, impulses, emotions, and cognitions, it's a lot easier to get caught up in the cognitions, and to stay there.

One of those cognitions might be, "This person is to blame for the way I feel." That might be completely valid. But we don't want to stay there, because when it comes to re-regulating, that story may not be serving that purpose, even though it's true, and valid, and important.
So the cognitions are significant, but they're a clue as to where we need to go. What I'm more interested in is: what's the flavor of that cognition?

Is it acceptance? "Yeah, I was mistreated, and that's why I feel like this." Is it an aha moment? Or is it, "Man, what an asshole. I can't believe they did that to me"? That might be valid too, and I can agree with you on that.

The flavor of it gives you an indication of what's happening inside of you. So I don't want you getting caught up in the thought, the story: this person is a jackass, they mistreated me, they're so narcissistic. Okay, that might be true. Fine. But is it a calm, stillness sort of reflecting on reality? Or is it a blaming, fight-flavored reflection of reality? The reality could still be true. It's more about what's driving it. What's the emotion, and ultimately the state, that's driving it?
Deb Dana said it when she was on the podcast:

q: You can see how the story changes dependent on the state, not depending on what I choose to think.
blocks.cite: Deb Dana, [Deb Dana Interview: Story Follows State, Climbing the Ladder and Diagnosing (episode 29)](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/f8b9643c-28f8-4185-9525-8b4e6301516c)

blocks.h: Link it down to the body

blocks.p: The word I use for this is linking. That cognition is directly connected to your polyvagal state. We just have to link it. Rather than getting caught up in the cognition:

ol: Link the cognition to the emotion that's driving it.
Link that emotion to the sensations, or the impulses, but usually the sensations.
Link that to an underlying impulse that needs to be completed, or acted upon, or felt.

blocks.p: The cognition that "this is why I'm dysregulated" can be valid and true. Cool. What's the flavor of it? Then dig deeper, from the cognition to the emotion, to the sensations, and ultimately, hopefully, down to the impulse underneath it. All of it anchored in safety, inching forward, one step at a time.
